standard.title: Locate and respond to key information in texts
standard.description: locate and respond to key information related to familiar content obtained from spoken, written and multimodal texts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can locate key information in familiar texts with support and respond using gestures, images, words and formulaic phrases (AC9LS2C03). They have not yet independently located information for research purposes, surveyed peers, or represented data from texts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students locate and respond to key information in familiar spoken, written and multimodal texts — including for research, data collection, comparison and presentation purposes.

nodes.label: Locating and categorising information from texts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can locate key information from a range of target language texts and categorise it using tables, charts and graphic organisers.
nodes.minimum_width: Locate specific information from at least two different text types and organise it into a graphic organiser or simple table.
nodes.typical_width: Listen for, read and view information in stories, reports, menus, advertisements and digital texts; categorise using tables, graphs and diagrams; survey classmates using familiar question forms; represent data in visual formats; use context and known vocabulary to locate information.
wider: Create a data representation from peer survey data — select the most appropriate format and explain what the data shows
Compare information from two different target language texts on the same topic — identify similarities, differences and what each includes that the other does not
nodes.hinge_reason: Independent information location across text types is the prerequisite for research and text response tasks. Students who can only locate information with direct teacher support cannot develop the semi-independent research skills that build across subsequent bands.

response_modes.reason: Information location skills develop through varied text types — different genres, modalities and topics present different comprehension challenges. Each new text type builds a new strategy.

success_criteria: Locates specific information from at least two different text types without direct teacher prompting
Organises located information into an appropriate graphic format

nodes.label: Responding to texts with personal reactions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can respond to target language texts — expressing personal reactions and opinions about characters, events and ideas.
nodes.minimum_width: Express a personal reaction to at least one text using target language evaluative expressions.
nodes.typical_width: Express reactions to characters, events and ideas in texts; act out character traits and sayings; answer questions about texts in the target language; respond to questions about people, places and ideas encountered in texts.
wider: Produce an extended text response — not only a personal reaction but a short comparative comment identifying what two characters or events have in common and how they differ
Respond to a First Nations Australian cultural story — expressing a personal reaction to its themes or characters in the target language

response_modes.reason: Evaluative response language develops through encountering varied texts and practising different response types. Students need a bank of evaluative expressions before they can respond genuinely rather than only neutrally.

success_criteria: Expresses a personal reaction to a text using at least one target language evaluative expression
Responds to at least two questions about a text using target language or English as appropriate

nodes.label: Adapting and recreating familiar texts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can adapt familiar target language texts for new purposes or audiences — substituting elements, resequencing events or creating alternative versions.
nodes.minimum_width: Produce at least one adaptation of a familiar text with at least two substituted elements (e.g. character, setting or event).
nodes.typical_width: Create adaptations of familiar stories and songs using substitution; adapt texts by changing location, character or ending; create invitations incorporating elements from stimulus texts; produce new versions of familiar rhymes or procedures.
wider: Create an adaptation that changes the cultural setting — moving a story or scenario to a different target language community context and explaining the changes made
Produce a collaborative text adaptation where each partner contributes different elements — demonstrating that both can create in the target language independently

response_modes.reason: Text adaptation is the earliest form of genuinely creative language use. Adapting across varied text types — stories, songs, procedures, invitations — builds the creative production capacity needed for original text creation.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Students who adapt texts are not copying — they are applying linguistic knowledge to construct something new. Width investment here builds creative production capacity that scales through the sequence.
success_criteria: Produces an adaptation of a familiar text with at least two substituted elements
The adapted text makes sense as a coherent whole — not just a list of substitutions
